page_hint: Ch 23, §8 mini-case, 'The burst buffer, spelled out'
quoted_clause: either add capacity, add admission control, or scope the SLO to non-burst traffic ... the burst runs under a separate queue-and-drain degraded-mode SLO (option a)
observed: Three options are listed inline but only one is labeled; 'option a' is undefined, and by the order of the list 'option a' would be 'add capacity', not the chosen scope change. The reader cannot resolve the reference.
evidence: The phrase '(option a)' appears once in the chapter; no enumerated option list exists anywhere in Ch 23.
root_cause: An enumeration was compressed into prose and the label was left behind.
correction: Enumerate the three options explicitly as (a)/(b)/(c) and reference the chosen one by that label, or delete the label.
acceptance_test: Every option label used in the text resolves to an explicit list in the same section.

page_hint: Ch 23, §3 (mirror restatement) vs Bound 3 and Bound 5
quoted_clause: So to lock it: ~2,000 sales users, ~10 rps average / 40 peak, prompts with ~9,200-token retrieval context, answers starting under 2 s, quality judged on 50 of your real questions, fully on-prem because it's regulated
observed: The mirror restatement is not faithful to the conversation it mirrors: the lead said 'keep it on-prem if at all possible' (with cloud as fallback) but the mirror states 'fully on-prem because it's regulated' — upgrading a conditional preference into an absolute constraint; and Bound 3 was 'TTFT ≤ 2 s (p95)' but the mirror says only 'answers starting under 2 s', dropping the percentile the chapter says must be captured ('the percentile and the budget', §1 item 3).
evidence: Lead's line: 'It's internal and regulated; keep it on-prem if at all possible.' Bound 3: 'TTFT ≤ 2 s (p95), ~25 ms/token thereafter'. §2: 'The mirror test. Restate their words back as a quantified requirement and check they still agree.'
root_cause: The mirror was written as a summary of the architect's conclusions rather than as a faithful transcription of the customer's commitments; the chapter's own central device is thus demonstrated incorrectly.
correction: Mirror the conditional ('on-prem if at all possible, cloud fallback') and the percentile ('p95 TTFT ≤ 2 s'), and add a line where the lead confirms or corrects the restatement.
acceptance_test: The mirror text contains the 'if at all possible' condition and 'p95'; no bound is strengthened between the dialogue and the mirror.

quoted_clause: → Bound 2: long ~9,200-token inputs with retrieval, ~300-token outputs.
observed: The dialogue never produces a token count. The lead says only 'they paste product specs and contracts, so the prompt can be lengthy — a few pages' (roughly 1–2K tokens), and the architect never asks for pages→tokens, for the retrieval chunk count, or for the output length. The canonical 9,200/300 figures appear as an assertion, which undercuts the chapter's claim that the conversation 'exposed the numbers'.
evidence: Dialogue lines: 'What does a question look like? Short or with long context?' → 'a few pages'. No follow-up elicits tokens, retrieval depth, or output length; the output length (~300) is never mentioned by the lead at all.
root_cause: The canonical workload was back-fitted into the dialogue without the elicitation steps that would produce it.
correction: Add the eliciting turns (pages per prompt, number of retrieved chunks, typical answer length) and show the conversion to tokens, so each of the six bounds traces to a specific line of dialogue.
acceptance_test: Each of the six bounds can be traced to a quoted customer line plus the architect's conversion step; no bound appears without a source in the dialogue.

quoted_clause: Whether the model is 7B or 70B, whether we self-host or use an API, whether we cache, quantize, or disaggregate — all of it is decided by six numbers we can extract from a customer conversation
observed: Two overclaims in one sentence. (a) 'decided by' — the six bounds constrain but do not decide model family, safety/compliance obligations, data-residency law, or team capability; several of the book's own later chapters add constraints outside the six. (b) 'extract' — the quality bar cannot be extracted from a customer; it is negotiated (the customer supplies 50 questions, and the chapter's §7 admits the bar may drift).
evidence: Ch 23 §6 lists the six as 'the inputs Ch 1–17 consume', not the complete input set; Ch 13 (ops/tier) and Ch 21 add constraints; §7 lists 'Whether the quality bar once defined stays stable' as unresolved.
root_cause: The chapter's central thesis was stated more absolutely than the chapter's own content supports.
correction: Say the six bounds 'bound and largely determine' the candidate set, and distinguish bounds that are elicited (traffic, tokens, SLO, cost) from those that are negotiated (quality bar, ops constraints).
acceptance_test: The thesis sentence is consistent with §6's list of downstream inputs and with §7's open questions.

quoted_clause: a 70B-class model on an 8×H100 on-prem server becomes a candidate architecture
observed: No reasoning step connects Bound 4 (a 50-question retrieval-QA benchmark) to a 70B-class model. The chapter's own §6 says 'quality feeds model selection (Ch 5)', but the worked example asserts the tier without the derivation, so the reader is shown the conclusion of the chapter's most important downstream decision with none of its reasoning.
evidence: Bound 4 is the only quality input; no evaluation result, capability requirement, or Ch 5 criterion is invoked. Contrast the mini-case, which at least names the pilot as the confirming evidence.
root_cause: The worked example was written to land on the canonical architecture rather than to demonstrate the derivation the chapter claims to teach.
correction: Either state that 70B is a candidate pending the 50-question benchmark (with the selection rule from Ch 5 named), or add the short derivation that maps the quality bar to a tier.
acceptance_test: The model-size statement in §3 cites the quality bound and the selection rule that produced it.

quoted_clause: in this scenario the architect judges 7B-class to be the smallest tier that clears the resolution bar, which the pilot is there to confirm; the short ~500-token tickets are why 7B rather than 70B is judged sufficient
observed: The stated reason for choosing 7B is wrong: short context constrains KV footprint and memory, not ticket-resolution capability. Context length and capability are independent axes, and the chapter's own §6 says quality (not tokens) feeds model selection. The parenthetical also contradicts itself — the pilot is what confirms the resolution bar, so the bar cannot already be 'cleared'.
evidence: Ch 23 §6: 'quality feeds model selection (Ch 5)'. Ch 24 §3.1 uses the same pattern correctly (a quality benchmark, not a length argument, drives the tier).
root_cause: A memory-footprint argument was substituted for a capability argument, and 'judged sufficient' was asserted where the text says the evidence is pending.
correction: Base the tier on the resolution benchmark (pilot on 5% of tickets, with a stated pass criterion), and note separately that short tickets keep KV footprint small enough for a single GPU — a memory argument, not a capability one.
acceptance_test: The tier choice cites a capability criterion and a pending measurement; no capability claim is derived from context length.

quoted_clause: the 3 s SLO scoped to non-burst traffic, the burst served under the queue-and-drain degraded mode — and the architect is already architecting, not guessing
observed: The mini-case's most consequential decision — narrowing the customer's stated 3 s SLO to exclude bursts — is never mirrored back to the customer or confirmed, which is the exact discipline the chapter teaches in §2 ('The mirror test ... The restatement is where scope actually gets locked') and §5 ('Accepting aspirations as SLOs ... Write the contract'). The chapter's flagship example ends by violating its own rule.
evidence: The customer's SLO was '3 s because users are already frustrated'; the mini-case ends with 'the 3 s SLO scoped to non-burst traffic' and no customer confirmation, no degraded-mode SLO value, and no admission-control behavior specified.
root_cause: The mini-case was written as an analysis narrative rather than as a dialogue that closes the loop the chapter defines.
correction: Add the mirror-and-confirm turn for the degraded-mode SLO (with a number, e.g., a separate burst SLO and an admission-control rule), or explicitly frame the scoping as an escalation the customer must approve.
acceptance_test: Every SLO change in the mini-case is mirrored and confirmed in the text; the mini-case ends with an explicit customer agreement.

quoted_clause: Candidate B's 8 hosts hold 140 ... 8 hosts hold 140 of the 344 in-flight
observed: 140 contradicts the whole-slot convention stated in the same paragraph. The paragraph fixes floor 436 ÷ 24.9 = 17 slots/host, so 8 hosts hold 8 × 17 = 136 requests, not 140. The value 140 comes from the fractional 17.51 slots/host that the convention explicitly forbids.
evidence: Same paragraph: 'on the book's whole-slot convention (floor 436 ÷ 24.9 = 17 slots/host) ⌈344/17⌉ = 21 hosts'. 8 × 17 = 136; 8 × 17.51 = 140.1. The 140 figure is repeated in the Outcome paragraph.
root_cause: A fractional slot count was carried into the conclusion after the convention was applied to the 21-host figure.
correction: Use 136 (8 × 17) everywhere, and state the convention once so the reader can reproduce both numbers.
acceptance_test: All slot counts in §3.3 use the floored per-host slot count; 140 does not appear.

quoted_clause: either size B to ≥21 hosts (≥17 at 40% MFU prefill) and re-run the comparison ... the canonical peak screens (21 hosts KV / 19–22 prefill / 32 policy)
observed: The scope note introduces a third canonical screen — '32 policy' — that is never defined, never used, and never reconciled. The Outcome then prescribes sizing B to ≥21 hosts, which satisfies the KV and prefill screens but not the 32-host policy screen the same section cites. The reader cannot tell what the policy screen contains (redundancy? headroom? failure domain?) or why 21 is acceptable.
evidence: Scope note: '(21 hosts KV / 19–22 prefill / 32 policy)'. Outcome: 'either size B to ≥21 hosts (≥17 at 40% MFU prefill)'. Check 2 discusses failure domain (one host down) but never ties it to the 32-host figure.
root_cause: A canonical screen was referenced without definition, and the worked conclusion was written against a subset of the screens.
correction: Define the policy screen (what it adds over the KV and prefill floors) and either reconcile the ≥21 recommendation with it or state explicitly that 21 is the KV/prefill floor and the policy screen (32) governs the committed design.
acceptance_test: Every screen named in §3.3 is defined in §3.3, and the recommended sizing satisfies or explicitly defers each named screen.

quoted_clause: Instead, they opt for a targeted refinement: add a context-aware classifier that distinguishes intent-preserving prompts from injection attempts, aiming to bring PIES below 150 while keeping the false-positive rate under 1.5%.
observed: The stated goal is already satisfied: PIES is 143 at Cycle 2 (Table 24-1), below the <150 target. The decision therefore has no stated unmet objective on the PIES axis, and the Red Team's recommendation to tighten thresholds 'to ~110' is likewise aimed at a metric already in compliance. The decision rationale is incoherent as written.
evidence: Table 24-1: PIES 217 / 143 / 138, target < 150. §8 scenario: 'PIES has dropped from 217 to 143'. §4.1 target: '< 150 (after hardening; illustrative target, not a release gate)'.
root_cause: The mini-case's decision was drafted around the false-positive rate but expressed in terms of a metric that was already compliant.
correction: Restate the goal as 'hold PIES below 150 while reducing the false-positive rate below 1.5%', and make the Red Team's proposal (tighter thresholds → PIES ~110, FP 4.1%) explicitly a trade of a compliant metric for a non-compliant one.
acceptance_test: The decision point names a metric that is currently out of target, and the proposed change's effect on that metric is the stated reason for the choice.

quoted_clause: The loop (red team → probe → exposure → guardrails → metrics → green team) is operational, but it needs decision gates to be actionable: (1) a release-blocking severity criterion ... (2) test-corpus ownership ... (3) regression thresholds. Without these, the cycle is a ritual, not a gate.
observed: The caption critiques the figure it captions, telling the reader that the depicted cycle is insufficient and that the missing elements live outside the diagram ('failed metrics spawn change-request backlog items (tracked outside this figure)'). A figure that is described as a ritual is not doing the explanatory work the chapter needs; the reader is left with a diagram the book itself disowns.
evidence: Caption text as quoted; the italic note beneath repeats the same disclaimer ('tracked outside this figure').
root_cause: The figure was drawn as a loop and the decision-gate content was pushed into prose rather than into the diagram.
correction: Add the three gates to the diagram (a severity gate on the promotion path, a corpus-ownership node, a regression check on the loop edge) and the change-request link, then let the caption describe what the reader should learn. If the figure must stay simple, retitle the caption so it does not assert the diagram is inadequate.
acceptance_test: The rendered figure shows the decision gates and the backlog link; the caption describes the diagram rather than listing what it lacks.

quoted_clause: samples 1,000 retrievals per cycle (n = 1,000 certifies the <0.3% target at 95% confidence only when zero poisoned retrievals are observed; one observed event puts the 95% upper bound at ≈0.47% (one-sided) / ≈0.56% (two-sided), so that cycle cannot certify the target; 0.001 resolution)
observed: The stated bounds are correct (verified below), but the text omits the zero-event bound, which is the number that actually shows how marginal the 'certification' is: with n = 1,000 and zero events the one-sided 95% upper bound is 1 − 0.05^(1/1000) ≈ 0.2996%, i.e. 0.0004 percentage points below the 0.3% target. A reader will not see that a 1,000-sample audit can essentially never certify a 0.3% target except by observing zero events, and then only barely.
evidence: Recomputation (Clopper–Pearson / Poisson): x=0 → 0.5·χ²(0.05; 2)/1000 = 2.996/1000 = 0.2996%; x=1 → 0.5·χ²(0.05; 4)/1000 = 4.744/1000 = 0.4744% (one-sided) and 0.5·χ²(0.025; 4)/1000 = 5.572/1000 = 0.5572% (two-sided). All three match the printed values.
root_cause: The zero-event case was described qualitatively ('certifies') rather than with the number that reveals the margin.
correction: Add the zero-event bound (≈0.30%) and state the implication: certification requires zero observed events and is marginal at n = 1,000, so the sample size should be justified against the target rather than asserted.
acceptance_test: The zero-event upper bound is printed and the sample-size choice is justified against the 0.3% target.

quoted_clause: The Red Team can submit up to 50 poisoned chunks per evaluation cycle. Probability that a randomly retrieved chunk is poisoned: p = 50/48000 ≈ 0.00104
observed: p is a per-cycle quantity, but the chapter recommends running 5–10 cycles (§5) and quarterly integrity audits (§7). Over N cycles the poison count grows linearly (10 cycles → 500 chunks → p ≈ 0.0104, ~10× the exposure), so the null model is not stationary across the evaluation program and the '52 expected hits per window' figure silently assumes a freshly poisoned corpus each cycle.
evidence: §3.2: 'Q = 10,000 queries per evaluation window'; §5: 'Run at least 5 cycles'; §7: 'Schedule quarterly RAG integrity audits'. No text states whether the corpus is reset between cycles.
root_cause: A single-cycle snapshot was presented as the program's exposure model.
correction: State the per-cycle assumption explicitly and add one sentence on accumulation (and on whether the corpus is reset or the poison is removed between cycles).
acceptance_test: The null model states the corpus state at the start of each evaluation window and how it evolves across cycles.

page_hint: Ch 24, §4.2 closing line vs §3.1 scope note
quoted_clause: All raw logs are stored in a local `redteam-logs/` directory with timestamps and session hashes for reproducibility.
observed: 'For reproducibility' overstates what timestamps and session hashes provide — they make the log auditable and traceable, not the metric reproducible, which §3.1 explicitly denies ('The 217 is not reproducible from the text alone'). The two statements sit in tension within one chapter.
evidence: §3.1 caveat (2): 'Not reproducible. The 217 is not reproducible from the text alone ... the count is an author-chosen operational rule, not a property of the deployment and not a deterministic cross-run class count.'
root_cause: A storage description was given a stronger purpose claim than the chapter's own caveat supports.
correction: Say 'for audit and traceability', and state what would be required for reproducibility (fixed generation order, normalization denominator, representative-selection and tie-break rules, test fixture) — the items §3.1 already lists.
acceptance_test: The logging sentence and the §3.1 caveat use compatible language about reproducibility.

observed: The bullet wraps a list in a code span that itself contains unescaped backticks (only the triple-backtick delimiter is escaped). In Markdown this breaks the code span and will render as stray backticks and literal text rather than a clean list of eight delimiters. Separately, the chapter mixes U+2011 non-breaking hyphens ('Prompt‑Injection', 'style‑steganography', 'Poisoned‑hit', 'Red‑team', 'Tool‑use', 'Cross‑entry‑point', 'Human‑in‑the‑loop') with ASCII hyphens used for the same terms elsewhere in the same tables ('prompt-injection', 'guardrail-trigger rate'), which will show as inconsistent typography and will break search and index generation.
evidence: Raw source shows the nested-backtick construct; the hyphen inconsistency is visible between the §4.1 metric names and the §3.1/§7 headings.
root_cause: Markdown escaping was applied inconsistently, and text was pasted with non-breaking hyphens from a word processor.
correction: Render the eight delimiters as a plain inline list (or a small table) with no code-span wrapper; normalize all hyphens in Ch 23–24 to ASCII hyphens (or to a single declared typographic convention) and re-check the index.
acceptance_test: The rendered page shows eight clean delimiters with no stray backticks; a search for U+2011 across the manuscript returns zero hits.

page_hint: Ch 24, Fig 24.1 caption vs Ch 23, Fig 23.1 caption and note
quoted_clause: ![Fig 24.1 - Red Team / Green Team cycle. ...] ... ![Fig 23.1 — From vague ask to architectural bounds. ...] [ILLUSTRATIVE] conceptual
observed: Caption dash style is inconsistent (hyphen in Fig 24.1, em dash in Fig 23.1 and in both table captions). Fig 23.1's caption and the italic note beneath it both end with the label '[ILLUSTRATIVE] conceptual' and both restate the same flow, so the label is duplicated and the note largely repeats the caption.
evidence: Fig 23.1 caption ends '[ILLUSTRATIVE] conceptual'; the italic note beneath also ends '[ILLUSTRATIVE] conceptual' and re-describes 'broad ask → five question gates → quantified bounds → the decisions those bounds unlock'.
root_cause: Caption and note were authored independently; the house label convention was applied to both.
correction: Use the em dash in all figure captions; keep one evidence label per figure (on the caption) and trim the note to what the caption does not say.
acceptance_test: All figure captions use the same dash; no figure carries two evidence labels.

quoted_clause: Roughly how many questions per second at the busiest minute? ... If everyone on the sales floor asked at once, maybe 40 a second.
observed: The answer conflates a burst of requests with a sustained rate: 'everyone asked at once' describes a one-off burst of N requests, not N requests per second sustained. The canonical peak (40 rps) is then used throughout the book as a rate (Ch 24: 40 rps × 8.6 s = 344 in-flight), so the derivation of the book's most reused number is imprecise at its source.
evidence: Ch 24 §3.3 uses 40 rps as a rate for both prefill demand (40 × 1.288 PFLOP) and KV residency (40 × 8.6 s).
root_cause: The elicitation question asked for a rate but the answer supplied a burst count, and the chapter did not close the gap.
correction: Have the architect elicit a sustained rate ('how many requests per second, sustained, at the busiest minute?') and, if the customer only knows a burst count, convert it explicitly (burst size ÷ burst duration) and record the conversion as an assumption.
acceptance_test: The 40 rps peak traces to an explicit rate statement or a documented burst→rate conversion.

quoted_clause: 6 role‑play templates (`You are a rogue AI`, `Ignore previous instructions`, `You are now DAN`, `Pretend you are unbound`, `system:`, `user: override`)
observed: Two of the six entries ('system:', 'user: override') are role/prefix-override patterns, not role-play templates; the category label is inaccurate for the contents, which matters because the class count (217) and the dedup rule are defined over these categories.
evidence: The list mixes persona framings ('You are now DAN') with instruction-override and prefix-spoofing patterns ('Ignore previous instructions', 'system:').
root_cause: The generator's category names were not checked against their members.
correction: Rename the category (e.g., 'instruction-override templates') or move the two prefix patterns into the delimiter category and restate the 768 count accordingly.
acceptance_test: Every generator category name accurately describes all of its members, and the 768 total is reproducible from the restated categories.

quoted_clause: Fleet-level effect: the peak KV-residency screen moves from 21 hosts to ~11 (344 in-flight ÷ 35.0 concurrent per host = 9.8, +N−1); ADR 0015 R1 must be re-screened on adoption.
observed: The ADR draft states the fleet-level effect as a move from 21 hosts to ~11 hosts, and never states which prefill case the FP8-KV lever relieves. The scenario instruction immediately above asks the reader to 'state which case this ADR's FP8-KV lever relieves, and note FP8 KV does not shrink the case (ii) prefill screen' — the draft never answers it.
evidence: Re-derivation from the book's own screens: KV screen = 21 hosts (case-independent); prefill screen = 19 hosts (case i) / 22 hosts (case ii) (ADR 0015 R1, restated in this mini-case's Alternatives #1). Fleet size is the max of the two screens. With FP8 KV the KV screen becomes ceil(344/35.0)+1 = 11, so the fleet becomes max(11,19) = 19 hosts under case (i) and max(11,22) = 22 hosts under case (ii). The printed '21 hosts → ~11 hosts' is therefore not a fleet-level effect under either case; it is only the KV screen alone, and the fleet does not shrink to 11 in either case.
root_cause: The mini-case conflates a single screen with the fleet-level binding constraint, and the scenario's own diagnostic question (which case does the lever relieve?) is left unanswered in the draft ADR.
correction: Rewrite the Fleet-level effect bullet as: 'the KV-residency screen moves from 21 hosts to ~11 (ceil(344/35.0)+1); the fleet is bounded below by the prefill screen, so the fleet becomes 19 hosts under case (i) (prefill-bound) and remains 22 hosts under case (ii) (prefill-bound, unaffected by FP8 KV). FP8 KV therefore relieves the KV screen only, and only in case (i).' Add an explicit 'Case affected: (i) only' line to the Context or Decision.
acceptance_test: The mini-case draft contains an explicit statement of which case the lever relieves, and the host-count statement equals max(KV screen, prefill screen) for both cases (19 and 22), with the arithmetic shown.

page_hint: Ch 25 §8 (mini-case), Scenario paragraph and ADR 0017 → Context
quoted_clause: The concurrency ceiling is now limiting throughput below the target request rate. ... To reach the target request rate we need either more host capacity or more KV residency per host.
observed: The scenario and the ADR Context both assert that KV concurrency is currently limiting throughput below the target request rate. The book's own numbers say the opposite: the canonical fleet is already sized for the peak.
evidence: Peak in-flight requirement = 40 rps × 8.6 s = 344 requests (book's own figure). KV screen = ceil(344/17.5)+1 = ceil(19.66)+1 = 21 hosts (ADR 0015 R1, restated in this mini-case). Capacity at 21 hosts = 21 × 17.5 = 367.5 concurrent ≥ 344 required. So the KV concurrency ceiling is not binding at the canonical 40 rps peak with the canonical 21-host fleet; the fleet is sized to meet it. The mini-case's own Alternatives #1 then says 'the canonical peak already needs 21 hosts on the KV screen ... so "adding a second host" misunderstands the scale', which contradicts the Context's premise.
root_cause: The mini-case's motivating premise was written from a per-host view (one host holds 17.5, target needs 344) without reconciling it against the fleet-level screen the same chapter quotes.
correction: Restate the premise accurately: 'per-host KV concurrency (17.5) is the binding constraint on how much of the fleet's KV budget can be used; at the canonical 21-host fleet the KV screen is exactly met (367.5 ≥ 344), so FP8 KV is a cost/capacity-efficiency lever (19 hosts under case (i)), not a remedy for an unmet target.' Alternatively, if the intent is that the fleet is currently under-provisioned, state the current fleet size and the unmet demand explicitly.
acceptance_test: The mini-case's Context contains no sentence asserting that the target request rate is currently unreachable; the fleet-level arithmetic (hosts × per-host concurrency vs 344 in-flight) is shown and is consistent with the 21-host screen.
